items.name: The sea in late October
items.teaser: October water in the bay averages about 19.5C and falls through the month; November is nearer 17C
items.story: The honest number for Cavalaire: the long-run October average for the sea is about 19.5C, with a range from roughly 16.7C to 22.2C depending on the year and the wind, and the bathing is described as cool rather than warm. Daily readings for 2022 to 2025 mostly sat between 19 and 22C. The old guide's November figure is about 17.3C: the water lags the air, so it stays milder than the evenings. A mistral turns the surface over and can take several degrees off in a day. The lifeguards and the beach clubs have gone; the Grande Plage is free and nearly empty.
items.why: Swim at midday after two calm days, never the morning after a mistral, and bring a wetsuit for anyone who feels the cold.

items.name: Mushrooms in the Maures: ask first
items.teaser: Ceps come after the autumn rain under the chestnuts and cork oaks, but every mushroom belongs to the landowner
items.story: After the first heavy autumn rains the chestnut and cork-oak woods of the Maures produce ceps and other mushrooms, and October and November are the season. The honest part is the law. Under the French Civil Code a mushroom belongs to the owner of the land it grows on, who may keep the picking or allow it, and much of the Maures is private estate. Rules on quantities are set department by department by prefectoral order, and no current Var order on picking was found when checked. In other departments picking beyond about ten litres can be prosecuted as theft.
items.why: Buy them at the market or eat them at a Maures table rather than filling a bag on someone's land.

bougie.title: 1431 — the fishermen who judge their own sea
bougie.desc: Why the boats sell off the quay, and the old fishermen's courts of the Provençal coast that still govern these waters.
bougie.lede: The fish sold off the quay at Cavalaire comes from a fleet that has never answered only to the state. Along this coast fishermen elect their own judges, the prud'hommes, an institution first recorded in Marseille in 1431, older than any royal ordinance and still at work in the waters of the bay today.
paras: The prud'homie is a fishermen's court. Skippers elect prud'hommes from among themselves, who share out the grounds, set gear and seasons, and settle disputes between boats. In Marseille the practice is recorded from 1431 and confirmed in 1477 by letters patent of King René; a 2025 press article gives 1452, so the founding date is argued. A decree of 19 November 1859, barely changed, still governs the thirty-three on the French Mediterranean, and the Ministry of Culture lists their practices as intangible heritage.

Each prud'homie has its own stretch of sea, fixed by decree. A Port-Cros national park study by Faget and Le Direach gives Saint-Tropez the waters from the Garonnette at Sainte-Maxime to Pramousquier beach near Cap Nègre, which takes in the bay of Cavalaire, and Le Lavandou those from the Pointe Blanche to the same beach. Saint-Tropez's archives run from 1770 to 1956. The study finds Cavalaire's shores, on the edge of both, full of quarrels between fishing communities from the late 18th century.

Cavalaire's port is attested in the 15th century, with its fishermen's houses. One tourism guide says its Maison des Pêcheurs houses a prud'homie created under Louis XIV; no official source for a separate Cavalaire prud'homie was found. Nor is the quay sale a royal privilege: Colbert's Ordonnance de la Marine dates from 1681, not 1652, and no article on direct sale was found. First sale now normally goes through a halle à marée under a 1989 decree, while small sales on the quay remain common.

_corrections: Colbert's Ordonnance de la Marine dates from August 1681, not 1652 (Colbert was not yet in office in 1652).

No article of the 1681 ordinance granting fishermen a right to sell directly without passing through the criée was found; the claim is dropped. Today first sale normally goes through a halle à marée (decree of 26 April 1989), and direct sale on the quay is a widespread small-scale practice, not an ancient privilege.

'A centuries-old prud'homie' is right in spirit but the origin is medieval, not Louis XIV: the practice is recorded at Marseille in 1431 and confirmed by King René in 1477 (one 2025 press source says 1452).

Which prud'homie covers Cavalaire: per the Port-Cros park study, the Saint-Tropez prud'homie's waters run from the Garonnette (Sainte-Maxime) to Pramousquier near Cap Nègre, which includes the bay of Cavalaire; Le Lavandou's run from the Pointe Blanche to Pramousquier. A tourism claim that Cavalaire has its own prud'homie created under Louis XIV is unconfirmed and kept as a dispute.
Prud'homies are governed by the decree of 19 November 1859; there are 33 on the French Mediterranean.
